01-001.r: Mixed economy → public sector and private sector co-exist in the national economy; blends market economy with planned economy.

01-004.r: Indian economy → mixed economy (its main characteristic); combines aspects of capitalism and socialism.
01-004.t: Don't confuse with socialist or Gandhian socialist economy; India is a mixed economy.

01-007.r: India → labour-surplus economy: large population and unlimited workers willing to work at a subsistence wage.

01-008.r: Underdeveloped economy → low per capita income and low rate of capital formation; low dependency ratio and tertiary-heavy workforce are not its features.

01-009.r: India underdeveloped → inequitable income distribution, high dependency ratio, slower national income growth; change in banking/financial sector is not a sign. Code: none of these.

01-010.r: Developing economy signs → occupation mainly agriculture, disguised unemployment, poor quality of human capital; high per capita protein intake is not one.

01-012.r: Indian economy → predominance of agriculture, low per capita income, massive unemployment; predominance of industry marks a developed economy, not India.

01-013.r: Indian economy → developing economy; at present a middle income developing market economy.

01-014.r: Not a feature of Indian economy → lack of natural resources; low labour productivity, low per capita income, low capital formation are features.

01-015.r: Voluntary social service → not an economic activity; farming, transportation and services are (input of resources → production → output).

01-016.r: Social behaviour → non-economic factor of growth; natural, energy and capital resources are economic factors.

01-017.r: Second Generation Economic Reforms → oil sector, public sector, government and public institutions reforms; legal (judicial) system reform is not included.

01-018.r: Indian model of development (mixed economy) → protects interests of both State (public sector) and Person (private sector).

02-001.r: National Income = NNP at factor cost = GNP at market prices – depreciation – indirect taxes + subsidies; NNP at market price = GNP – depreciation.
02-001.h: Market price → factor cost: subtract indirect taxes, add subsidies.

02-005.r: NNP = GNP – Depreciation; GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad; so NNP = GDP + NFIA – Depreciation (both correct).

02-006.r: National income → money value of all final goods and services produced by normal residents of a country in a period (generally one year).

02-007.r: Open economy national income → Y = C + I + G + (X – M); X – M = net exports.

02-008.r: GDP methods → Product, Income, Expenditure; 'diminishing cost method' is not one.

02-009.r: NNP and GNP → both measure the money value of national production, and the two are different.
02-009.c: Book gives no single answer: it says both (a) and (d) are correct, since GNP and NNP both measure national output in money but differ by depreciation.

02-010.r: Nominal GDP → GDP at current market prices, without inflation adjustment; used to find the GDP deflator and real GDP.
02-010.t: Don't confuse with real GDP, which is valued at constant prices.

02-011.r: Main problem in calculating India's national income → non-organized sector (no proper records); also unreliable data and double counting.

02-012.r: NDP = GDP – Depreciation (not plus); none of the three statements (NDP formula, per capita income = NDP/population, NDP better for comparison) is true.

02-013.r: Personal Disposable Income (PDI) = Personal income – Personal tax payments (direct taxes); it is spent or saved.

02-014.r: Prices and money income both doubled → real income unchanged.

02-015.r: Economic growth measured by growth in GDP, GNP and per capita GNP; growth in World Bank financial aid is not considered.

02-016.r: Amartya Sen's priorities for India → people-oriented (not commodity-oriented), economic security to poorest of the poor, safeguards against integration with world economy.

02-017.r: 'Planning should pay more attention to people than to commodities' → Amartya Sen (Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, 1998).

02-018.r: Hindu rate of growth → slow growth of National Income/GDP (about 3.5%, 1950s–1980s); term first used by Prof. Raj Krishna, 1981.

02-020.r: Economic growth → usually coupled with inflation (rising income raises demand for goods).

02-021.r: Labour's share in GNP becomes low when wages lag behind prices.

02-022.r: Economic development → constructive change; economic growth → GDP; sustainable development → environment; quality of life → health.

02-023.r: Last decade: public sector's share in GDP declined (private sector's rose) → true; GDP increased four times in 10 years → false.

02-024.r: Boom → high business activity, rising income, output, employment; recession → gradual fall, business in low gear; depression → unprecedented unemployment, drastic fall; then recovery.

02-025.r: Meltdown → steep fall in stock prices (only correct pair); recession → massive contraction of economic activity; slowdown → decrease in economic activity.

02-026.r: New Economic Policy 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) is criticised by insiders and outsiders, largely on ideological grounds → A and R true, R explains A.

02-028.r: Liberalisation began with changes in industrial licensing → New Industrial Policy, 24 July 1991 (Narsimha Rao govt); all except 18 industries freed from licence.

02-029.r: NEP: stabilisation → quick, demand-side (inflation, fiscal, balance of payments); structural adjustment → gradual multi-step, supply-side (trade, capital flow, industrial reforms).

02-030.r: Pioneer of liberalisation of Indian economy → Dr. Manmohan Singh, Finance Minister in 1991.
02-030.t: Don't pick P.V. Narsimha Rao; the 'pioneer' title goes to Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.

02-031.r: India's occupational structure stayed nearly the same → investment pattern directed towards capital-intensive industries.

02-032.r: Real sector (production and flow of goods) → farmers harvesting crops, textile mills making fabric; bank lending and overseas rupee bonds → financial sector.

02-033.r: Major growth factors → natural resources, physical capital, population/labour, human capital, technology, law; technocrats and bureaucrats are not.

02-034.r: Sign of economic growth and best index of development → sustained increase in real per capita income (year to year).

02-036.r: Most appropriate measure of economic growth and of standard of living → per capita real income (Per Capita Product / per capita NNP).

02-038.r: Higher absolute and per capita real GNP is not higher development if poverty and unemployment increase; development = growth + better living standards.

02-039.r: Per capita income grows faster at current prices than at constant prices → constant prices remove the increase in price level (inflation).

02-040.r: First estimate of India's national income → Dadabhai Naoroji, 1867-68; per capita income Rs. 20.

02-041.r: National Income Committee, 1949 → chairman P.C. Mahalanobis; members D.R. Gadgil and V.K.R.V. Rao.

02-042.r: First scientific estimate of national income → Dr. V.K.R.V. Rao (1931-32); first attempt → Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68).
02-042.t: Don't confuse the first attempt (Naoroji) with the first scientific estimate (V.K.R.V. Rao).

02-043.r: National Income data → earlier CSO (set up 1951); now National Statistical Office (NSO), formed by merging CSO and NSSO.

02-047.r: Capital formation data → RBI and Central Statistical Organisation (now NSO); roles set by K.N. Raj Committee (1981) on saving and investment estimates.

02-048.r: Base year → the year whose prices are used to calculate real GDP (constant prices); present base year 2011-12.

02-049.r: 2015: CSO changed both base year (2004-05 → 2011-12) and method (GVA at basic prices replaced GDP at factor cost).

02-052.r: GDP base year at constant prices → 1999-2000 when this was asked; later 2011-12, since replaced by a newer base year.
02-052.c: Book gives no single answer, but its explanation shows (a) 1999-2000 was the base year when this was asked.

02-053.r: National income base year → 2004-05 when this was asked; later 2011-12, since replaced by a newer base year.
02-053.c: Book gives no single answer, but its explanation shows (c) 2004-05 was the base year when this was asked.

02-054.r: CSO's new GDP series, February 1999 → base prices of 1993-94 (present base year 2011-12).

02-055.r: Economic development needs a multi-dimensional approach (A true); government focuses on both micro and macro issues, not mainly micro (R false).

02-056.r: Per capita income 2009-10 (rose 14.5%) → about Rs. 46,500 (Economic Survey: Rs. 46249 at current prices).

02-057.r: Per capita NNI 2013-14 (current prices, factor cost) → Rs. 79118 (new series), so none of the options.

02-058.r: Highest per capita income growth at constant prices (2004-05 series), 1951-52 to 2015-16 → 2007-08 (8.6%).

02-059.r: Per capita income 2010-11 at 2004-05 prices (Quick Estimates) → Rs. 35,993.
